title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students perceive ChatGPT when it is used as a virtual tutor in a physics course. The authors were concerned with whether students trust ChatGPT’s answers, whether that trust is related to answer accuracy, and how trust shapes students’ broader perceptions of the tool. The study is framed around the opportunities and risks of generative AI in education, especially the possibility that students may overtrust incorrect outputs and develop misconceptions about AI.

The intervention was a make-up exam assignment embedded in an introductory college physics class. After taking a 50-item multiple-choice exam on light, radioactivity, and related topics, students used ChatGPT to work through the questions they answered incorrectly. They followed a structured chat flow, could ask additional questions, and then completed a survey about perceived usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use ChatGPT in the future. Students were also asked to draw a visual representation of ChatGPT, which was used to analyze anthropomorphic perceptions and warmth.

The study took place at a public university in the southern United States with 40 undergraduates, most of whom had little prior experience with ChatGPT. Quantitatively, ChatGPT answered 85% of the questions correctly, yet many students still trusted its responses even when they were wrong. Trust was associated with more positive perceptions, especially higher perceived ease of use and future intention to use. Qualitatively, students often depicted ChatGPT as a robot, machine, or super-intelligent entity, revealing misconceptions such as anthropomorphism and the belief that AI is infallible.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT can function as a virtual tutor, but its use requires caution because incorrect answers can reinforce misconceptions. They argue for stronger AI literacy instruction, explicit teaching of critical evaluation and prompt engineering, and more transparent or explainable AI design. They also caution against making educational GenAI systems too anthropomorphic or overly persuasive, since such design features may encourage blind trust.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with survey, clustering, ANOVA, MANOVA, and qualitative drawing analysis, but it is not an experimental comparison of learning outcomes and has limited generalizability (single class, small sample). Evidence credibility is therefore correlational/mixed-method rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a moderate association between trust and perceptions, but no direct learning gain effect and clear risks from inaccurate answers and overtrust. Overall impact on learning is plausible but unclear, with both benefits and harms documented.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual tutor/assistant in an introductory physics class to answer students' exam questions during a makeup assignment and provide follow-up explanations in a chat-based interaction.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 85% of physics questions correctly overall (307/362), but 15% were incorrect and the model sometimes changed answers when probed further. The study focused on students' ability to use ChatGPT to address physics questions on light and radioactivity, showing usefulness as a tutor but meaningful accuracy and reliability risks for scientific problem-solving.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics questions; correctness of students' agreement with responses

finding.finding_summary: Students' trust in ChatGPT was associated with their perceptions of the system, and many students showed strong trust even when answers were wrong. The paper highlights misconceptions, critical-thinking risks, and the need for AI literacy and prompt engineering, indicating both potential support and substantial risk for judgment and evaluation skills.
finding.measure: Trust levels, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, intention to use, and drawing-based perceptions of ChatGPT
